title: Robotics: Foundations of future labour
description: Send us Fan Mail An hour long 'Brucey bonus' episode this week (and make sure to listen to the bitter end for our first AI created outro track ' Robot Visions ') Join Matt Cartwright and Jimmy Rhodes as they unfold the future of robotics and its intersection with everyday life. This week, we're tearing down the walls between human and machine, exploring the burgeoning potential of robots like Figure 01 by Figure AI and their integration with large language models. Witness the thought-provoking discussion on how companies like Boston Dynamics and Google are not just shaping the aesthetic of tomorrow's robots but also paving the way for these machines to seamlessly mingle with our environment. As we sail through the captivating world of AI development, we'll tackle the concept of reward functions and their role in the astonishing advancement of AI capabilities. NVIDIA is at the forefront, pushing the boundaries with virtual training environments and AI-driven chip design – but at what cost? This episode isn't shy about addressing the dual-edged sword of data control, consumer autonomy, and the looming question of AI sustainability in energy consumption. Matt and Jimmy take you beyond the code, into the ethics and societal impacts of AI in our homes and workplaces. But what is human cost? As automation redefines the workforce, we grapple with the redistribution of labor, the potential of a 32-hour workweek, and the influence of collective action in an automated era. From the quiet revolution in agriculture and logistics to the potential backlash against domestic robots, the conversation gets real about the future of jobs in the AI age. Are human-centric professions safe? Can universal basic income be the answer? Matt and Jimmy don't just ask the tough questions – they confront the realities of a world on the brink of an AI work revolution.
summary: The robotics deep-dive covers Figure 01's demo with OpenAI, Boston Dynamics' drumming robot and Nvidia's virtual training worlds, concluding that robotics lags LLMs by roughly a year but is accelerating through the same neural-network paradigm — reward functions now being written by LLMs. They wrestle with Amazon's 750,000 robots and its opaque 'safety' math, debate UBI versus robot taxes on model providers, and land on gradual displacement, union-driven backlash, and safety as the gatekeeper for home robots.
keyTalkingPoints: Figure 01 (OpenAI-powered) and Boston Dynamics' drumming robot show multimodal embodiment arriving; Nvidia trains robots in virtual worlds
The singularity feedback loop is visible now: reward functions for robots increasingly written by LLMs; we do not program neural networks, we let them learn
Amazon's Sequoia announcement: 750,000 robots and a confusing safety claim that robots reduce injuries — the hosts cannot parse the math
Displacement math is crude: 100 million robots a year is not one-per-one replacement, and rollout will be gradual like the car fleet
Finances: Matt floats UBI funded by taxing AI providers rather than robots; offshore model companies make that hard
Backlash will run through unions; home robots live or die on safety and trust — 'maybe in 10 years the robots will have gone ape'

jimmy: Robotics is further away than LLMs but heading the same way — the pace of recent announcements is exponential
The gradual path is like the global car fleet: robots enter piecemeal, and companies will never admit cuts are because of AI
Genuine copium: robots can take jobs people do not want — exploitation jobs, dangerous work, underserved industries
Social jobs grow, not shrink, in a robot world — even if that includes robot masseurs and counselors
matt: Humanoid robots still look frightening; the replacement arithmetic in the news does not add up and deserves scrutiny
Every PC and data center without AI integration is now effectively obsolete — chips are evolving that fast
Funding the transition needs radical options: UBI, or a robot tax levied on the model providers instead
Unionization is the realistic brake on robotics; people will not allow unsafe robots into their homes
